## Introduction

Can a few yes/no questions about a tumor's measurements tell benign from
malignant? That is a decision tree. In this lab we use R packages to fit a
single tree, prune it, and then improve it with bagging, random forests and
boosting. Same data as Lab 9: 569 tumors, 30 features.

Click **Run Code** on each cell, in order.

## Data

We keep 30% of the tumors as a test set.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(gbm)

wdbc <- read.csv("data/wdbc.csv") |>
  mutate(diagnosis = factor(diagnosis, levels = c("B", "M"),
                            labels = c("Benign", "Malignant")))

set.seed(2155)
idx   <- createDataPartition(wdbc$diagnosis, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train <- wdbc[idx, ]
test  <- wdbc[-idx, ]

acc <- function(pred) mean(pred == test$diagnosis)   # test accuracy
```

# 1. A classification tree

`rpart()` does recursive binary splitting, choosing each split by the Gini
index. We first let it grow a large tree ($T_0$ in the slides).

```{webr}
set.seed(2155)
big <- rpart(diagnosis ~ ., data = train,
             control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2, xval = 10))

rpart.plot(big, type = 2, extra = 0, box.palette = c("#3B4992", "#EE0000"),
           split.cex = 0.9, branch = 0.5, clip.facs = TRUE)
acc(predict(big, test, type = "class"))
```

# 2. Pruning

`cp` is the cost-complexity penalty $\alpha$ (a larger `cp` gives a smaller
tree). `rpart` already ran 10-fold CV for each `cp` while growing the tree.
We pick the `cp` with the lowest CV error (`xerror`) and prune back to it.

```{webr}
printcp(big)
plotcp(big)

best_cp <- big$cptable[which.min(big$cptable[, "xerror"]), "CP"]
pruned  <- prune(big, cp = best_cp)

rpart.plot(pruned, type = 4, extra = 104, under = TRUE, box.palette = c("#3B4992", "#EE0000"), tweak = 1.3)
acc(predict(pruned, test, type = "class"))
```

**Check:** how many leaves does the pruned tree have compared with the large
tree? Did test accuracy change?

# 3. Bagging

Bagging is a random forest in which every split may use all $p$ features
(`mtry = p`). The package also gives the out-of-bag (OOB) error for free.

```{webr}
set.seed(2155)
bag <- randomForest(diagnosis ~ ., data = train, mtry = 30, ntree = 500)

bag                                   # includes the OOB error and confusion matrix
acc(predict(bag, test))
```

# 4. Random forest

A random forest allows only $m \approx \sqrt{p}$ randomly chosen features at
each split, which decorrelates the trees.

```{webr}
set.seed(2155)
rf <- randomForest(diagnosis ~ ., data = train, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)

rf                                    # default mtry = sqrt(30), about 5
acc(predict(rf, test))

varImpPlot(rf, type = 2, n.var = 10)  # total decrease in Gini, per feature
```

**Check:** compare the OOB error of `bag` and `rf`. Which features matter most?

# 5. Boosting

Boosting grows trees one after another, each fit to what the previous trees
got wrong. `n.trees` is $n_B$, `shrinkage` is $\lambda$, and
`interaction.depth` controls the size $d$ of each tree.

```{webr}
train_b <- train |> mutate(y = as.numeric(diagnosis == "Malignant"), diagnosis = NULL)

set.seed(2155)
boost <- gbm(y ~ ., data = train_b, distribution = "bernoulli",
             n.trees = 500, interaction.depth = 2, shrinkage = 0.05, verbose = FALSE)

p_boost <- predict(boost, test, n.trees = 500, type = "response")
acc(factor(ifelse(p_boost > 0.5, "Malignant", "Benign"), levels = levels(test$diagnosis)))

summary(boost, n.trees = 500, plotit = FALSE)[1:10, ]   # variable importance
```

# 6. Compare

```{webr}
data.frame(
  model = c("Large tree", "Pruned tree", "Bagging", "Random forest", "Boosting"),
  test_accuracy = round(c(
    acc(predict(big, test, type = "class")),
    acc(predict(pruned, test, type = "class")),
    acc(predict(bag, test)),
    acc(predict(rf, test)),
    acc(factor(ifelse(p_boost > 0.5, "Malignant", "Benign"), levels = levels(test$diagnosis)))
  ), 3)
)
```

## Try it yourself

Change `mtry` in the random forest (try 2, 5, 10, 30). How do the OOB error and
test accuracy move?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mtry
set.seed(2155)
rf2 <- randomForest(diagnosis ~ ., data = train, mtry = ______, ntree = 500)
rf2
acc(predict(rf2, test))
```

## Things worth remembering

- A tree splits the feature space into regions with recursive binary splitting,
  and predicts the majority class (or the mean) in each region.
- A large tree overfits. Prune it with cost-complexity pruning, choosing the
  penalty by cross-validation.
- Bagging averages trees grown on bootstrap samples. The out-of-bag
  observations give an error estimate with no extra fitting.
- Random forests also sample the features at each split, which decorrelates the
  trees.
- Boosting grows trees sequentially on the previous errors.
- The ensembles usually predict better than one tree, but they are harder to
  interpret. Variable importance recovers some of the interpretation.
